title: Voiced H-Row — ば び ぶ べ ぼ

points.name: ば
points.explanation: The syllable ば is the voiced version of は — add a dakuten to は and the 'h' transforms into a 'b', producing a 'ba' sound as in 'bar' or 'back'. This is a particularly striking transformation: the breathy 'h' becomes a hard, voiced stop 'b' with the addition of two little strokes. ば is essential grammar: the conditional form of Japanese verbs ends in ば (e.g., たべれば = 'if you eat'). ば also appears in key vocabulary: ばしょ (place / location), さぼる (to skip / to slack off), and いばる (to be arrogant / to show off).
rules: ば = は + dakuten; the 'h' becomes 'b'. A dramatic change from a breathy fricative to a stop!
The ば conditional: verb stem + ば = 'if you [verb]'. たべれば = 'if (you) eat'.
Don't confuse ば with ぱ (coming next chapter) — ば has dakuten (゛), ぱ has handakuten (゜).

examples.english: to skip / to slack off / to play truant
to be arrogant / to show off / to boss around

points.flashcardAnswer: ba — like the 'ba' in 'bar' (voiced version of は)

points.name: び
points.explanation: The syllable び is the voiced version of ひ — the breathy 'h' before 'ee' becomes a firm 'b' before 'ee', producing a 'bi' sound like the start of 'bead' or 'beam'. び appears in lovely vocabulary: びじゅつかん (art museum), びょういん (hospital — びょ is a combination character), and the exclamation びっくり (surprised!). The character び looks identical to ひ but with dakuten marks added. びっくりした! (I was surprised!) is one of those expressions you'll hear constantly in anime and daily conversation.
rules: び = ひ + dakuten; 'h' before 'ee' becomes 'b' before 'ee'.
び appears in びじゅつ (fine art) and びっくり (surprised!) — culturally useful vocabulary.
The voiced 'b' is fully stops the airflow: lips close completely, then release with a buzz.
points.flashcardAnswer: bi — like the 'bi' in 'bead' (voiced version of ひ)

points.name: ぶ
points.shortDescription: Like 'boo' but with flat, unrounded lips
points.explanation: The syllable ぶ pairs the voiced 'b' with the Japanese unrounded 'u' vowel. It sounds like 'bu' — somewhere between English 'boo' and 'buh', since the 'u' vowel is flat rather than rounded. ぶ appears in important vocabulary: ぶんか (culture), ぶた (pig), ぶどう (grapes), and さぼる (derived from the French word 'sabotage'!). An interesting fact: many Japanese words for animals and plants use voiced consonants like ぶ and ぼ — perhaps reflecting the slightly heavier, earthier quality of voiced sounds.
rules: ぶ = ふ + dakuten; the unique bilabial 'f' of ふ becomes the bilabial stop 'b'.
Keep lips relaxed after the 'b' — unrounded Japanese 'u', not 'boo'.
ぶた (pig), ぶどう (grapes), and ぶんか (culture) are useful vocabulary words.

examples.english: (see ぶ in: なかまにはいる = to join a group)

points.name: べ
points.explanation: The syllable べ is the voiced version of へ — the 'h' becomes 'b', giving a 'be' sound like the beginning of 'bed' or 'bell'. べ appears in one of the most important verbs for learners: べんきょうする (to study — べんきょう = study), and in the instruction べつに (in particular / not especially). べ is also part of たべる (to eat), where the 'be' sound is natural and easy. たべる is one of the very first verbs most Japanese learners pick up, making べ immediately practical.
rules: べ = へ + dakuten; the directional 'h' sound becomes 'b'.
たべる (to eat) and べんきょう (study) are two of the most essential learner vocabulary words.
べつに (not particularly / not especially) is a useful conversational expression.

examples.english: to line up / to arrange in a row

points.flashcardAnswer: be — like the 'be' in 'bed' (voiced version of へ)

points.name: ぼ
points.explanation: The syllable ぼ is the voiced version of ほ — the 'h' becomes 'b' before the 'oh' vowel, giving a 'bo' sound like the start of 'bone' or 'bold'. ぼ appears in highly useful vocabulary: ぼうし (hat / cap), ぼく (I / me — male casual pronoun), ぼんやり (vaguely / absentmindedly), and ぼる (to overcharge — a useful word for tourists!). ぼく is particularly notable because it's one of the main first-person pronouns in Japanese, used predominantly in casual male speech and common in anime and manga.
rules: ぼ = ほ + dakuten; 'h' before 'oh' becomes 'b' before 'oh'.
ぼく (I / me) is a very common casual male pronoun — heard constantly in anime and casual conversation.
ぼうし (hat) is one of the first clothing vocabulary words most learners pick up.

examples.english: I see! / indeed (ほ+ど here for reference)

points.flashcardAnswer: bo — like the 'bo' in 'bone' (voiced version of ほ)

chapterPractice.prompt: The B-row characters (ば び ぶ べ ぼ) are voiced versions of which row?
chapterPractice.japanese: ば び ぶ べ ぼ
choices: K-row (か き く け こ)
S-row (さ し す せ そ)
H-row (は ひ ふ へ ほ)
T-row (た ち つ て と)
chapterPractice.explanation: The B-row comes from the H-row + dakuten (゛). は→ば, ひ→び, ふ→ぶ, へ→べ, ほ→ぼ. This is quite a dramatic change — from the breathy 'h' sounds to the firm 'b' stops.

chapterPractice.prompt: Which character makes the 'be' sound (as in 'bed')?
chapterPractice.explanation: べ makes the 'be' sound (like 'bed'). It's the voiced version of へ. You'll use べ in たべる (to eat) and べんきょう (study) — two essential beginner words.
たべる (taberu) means 'to eat'. た (ta) + べ (be) + る (ru) = taberu. This is one of the very first verbs Japanese learners encounter and use every day.
ぼうし (boushi) means 'hat' or 'cap'. ぼ (bo) + う (u) + し (shi) = boushi. The うin the middle creates a long 'o' sound — so it's pronounced 'boo-shi' (two beats for the 'o').
